conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’ve been vomiting all day and can’t keep anything down—not even water. It’s been like this since this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a history of gastroparesis, right? Is this similar to your past episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly like before. But this time, I stopped taking my Reglan because the pharmacy didn’t have the generic, and my insurance wouldn’t cover the brand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could definitely make things worse. Not taking your metoclopramide likely contributed to this flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so that’s why I’m feeling so bad again? I didn’t realize it was that important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It really is. It helps your stomach empty properly. We’ll get you back on it right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I’ve also been feeling really dizzy and my heart’s racing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s probably from dehydration. Your heart rate was elevated when you arrived. We’re giving you IV fluids to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. I haven’t had anything to drink all day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve also started you on anti-nausea medications—Zofran, Compazine, and Ativan—to help settle your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken Compazine at home before. It helps a little, but not completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using a combination now to get better control. Your labs show your blood sugar was high—330—when you came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s been hard to manage when I can’t eat. I didn’t know how much insulin to take.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ve lowered your Lantus dose temporarily because you’re not eating much. We’ll adjust it as you start tolerating food again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. Should I still take my sliding scale insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep the sliding scale. The diabetes team will help fine-tune it as your intake improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my blood pressure? I’ve been off my clonidine patch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned you stopped it because you weren’t sure if it was safe with lisinopril?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I thought maybe they were too similar. I didn’t want to drop my pressure too low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They work differently, so it’s safe to take both. We’re restarting the clonidine patch today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’m glad to hear that. I’ve had high readings at home lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor it closely. Your exam shows no abdominal pain, and your liver tests are normal, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain, just the nausea and vomiting. I’m just so tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with dehydration and poor intake. The fluids should help you feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I haven’t vomited since last night, and I sipped some ginger ale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’re going to try advancing your diet—start with toast and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat regular food soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go step by step. If toast goes well, we’ll try soup later. We also gave you a handout on a gastroparesis-friendly diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll make sure it fits with my diabetes plan too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your blood sugar was 145 this morning—much better. We’ll keep adjusting your insulin as you eat more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m worried about it spiking once I start eating again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you manage that. Your Lantus dose will go back up gradually. Follow the sliding scale we provided.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your heart rate has normalized, and labs show your hydration is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep tolerating food and fluids, yes. We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’re stable and tolerating toast and ginger ale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue taking your metoclopramide four times a day. If nausea returns, use Compazine as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow the sliding scale. As your eating improves, you may need to increase your Lantus—call your doctor to adjust it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Any other instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep your follow-up with your gastroenterologist in two months. If symptoms return or you have pacer concerns, go to their clinic any afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I remember that from last time. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, if you develop fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing, seek help right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’m just glad to be feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home with a prescription for metoclopramide—make sure you get the generic this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my lesson there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Take it slow with your diet, stay hydrated, and keep up with your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed, but I hope you stay on track.
